title: Rehabilitating Memory in Education
author: Jonathan Firth
summary: For his 150th post, Jonathan Firth summarizes a talk given at a memory-and-education seminar in Scotland, arguing that educators' suspicion of memory rests on outdated or oversimplified ideas. He traces the roots of memory research from Locke, Aristotle and Plato through Ebbinghaus and notes that early studies using meaningless stimuli encouraged a computer-like picture and an association with cramming and behaviourist drill. Educators' complaints that assessment rewards "memorisation" or that learning is not "committing facts to memory" echo the idea that generic skills can be taught without subject knowledge. Modern psychology instead sees many types of memory, organized in interconnected schemas and central to everyday problem solving. Firth concludes that memory is deeply integrated with thinking and with identity, shaped by autobiographical memories, the availability heuristic and confirmation bias, and so cannot be separated from understanding.
points: Memory matters for everything we learn and not only for last-minute cramming or shallow memorisation, so criticism of memorisation often targets a caricature.
Educators' wariness of memory partly traces to early research with meaningless stimuli and to associations with behaviourist conditioning, even though most behaviourists did not use the term.
Statements such as "learning is not committing facts to memory" lean on the idea that generic transferable skills can be taught without subject knowledge.
Modern cognitive psychology recognizes many types of memory, organized in schemas and used constantly in problem solving, rather than separate items in storage.
Memory shapes how we perceive and think through autobiographical memories, availability judgments and confirmation bias, so it is integrated with thinking and identity.
quotes: From a psychological point of view, however, memory is not something that only becomes relevant when preparing for exams, and it is not only useful for shallow memorisation. Everything that we learn involves using human memory in some way.
There is much overlap between the views of memory developed by early philosophers and how we now view memory in cognitive psychology.
These include Locke’s view of memory as storage, Aristotle’s view that memory and ‘recollection’ (i.e. retrieval) are two separate processes, and Plato’s views on individual differences in memory.

Linking concerns about memory/memorisation among educators to some early memory research that used meaningless stimuli (such as random words) or which oversimplified some aspects of the memory process, presenting it as more computer-like than it actually is.
A lot of this, of course, smacks of the idea that generic transferrable skills can be taught without a focus on subject knowledge, which was the focus of the final part of my talk.
We recognise that there are many different types of memory underlying a range of functions (from physical skills to habits to meaningful understanding).
We also know that memories are interconnected in schemas (see update #59) rather than being separate items, and that memories play a key role in everyday problem solving.
All of this points to a psychology of memory that is deeply integrated with thinking and with our identity.
